title: The Seventh Bell
subtitle: The Legend of Khalvar
teaser: For three hundred years nothing came to the Pass of Seven Bells. Then forty thousand came at once, the soldiers ran, and the only ones left to meet them were a statue, a bell, and the ten-year-old girl who rang it.

sections.heading: I. The Ringer’s Game
paragraphs: Every morning at first light, Vreni Holt climbed the hundred and nine steps of the gate tower and shouted the ringer’s call down the valley.
“First light, and the pass holds!”
Then she rang the Gate Bell, and far below, one after another, six smaller bells answered. Then she came back down, put her shoulder against the Warden’s knee, and pushed.
“Move,” she said.
He didn’t. He hadn’t moved in three hundred years.

The mason-priests of Khal Dur had cut him out of the mountain’s own flank, a giant of grey stone set in the gate arch like a door that had decided to stand up. They named him Khalvar and gave him one command: hold the Pass of Seven Bells. They gave him no weapon. A wall, the priests said, doesn’t need one.
For three hundred years, nothing came. Snow piled on his shoulders every winter and slid off every spring.
Vreni was ten. Her grandfather’s knees had given out, and nobody else would climb a hundred and nine frozen steps in the dark for a copper a week. So the bell was hers.

She talked to the Warden the way children talk to dogs, constantly and without waiting for answers. She told him which goats were in kid and which boys were idiots. She taught him the names of the six bells down the valley: the Widow, Kettle, Hare, Long Tom, Little Agnes, and Tin Jack by the mill, who was always late.

Nobody had ever heard him speak. But Vreni was the first person in three hundred years to ask him a question and then wait. She asked if he got cold, and sat on his foot all morning, and just before noon a voice came up out of the stone like a millstone turning.
“No.”
After that there was no stopping her.
“What are you for?”
“To hold the pass.”
“Against what?”
“Whatever comes.”
“Nothing comes.”
The Warden thought about this until the next morning. “Then I am doing well.”
That winter, something came.

sections.heading: II. The Ashen Host
paragraphs: The fires came first, covering the northern slopes from ridge to ridge. The Ashen Host smeared their faces with the ash of every town they had burned on the way, and there were forty thousand of them.
The valley’s hundred and twenty soldiers, in blue coats with brass buttons, ran on the second night. The Warden watched their lanterns bob away down the road and didn’t blame them.
In three hundred years of watching people, he had learned one thing about them. They broke very easily. A person was a bag of warm water with a few sticks in it, and forty thousand was a great many.
The valley fled after the soldiers. Nearly all of it.
“The ringer doesn’t leave the tower,” Vreni told her mother. “If the bell stops, everyone thinks the pass has fallen.”

Her grandfather said the girl was right, and stayed with her. Down the valley, the other ringers stayed too, without anyone asking: a blind man at Kettle, two brothers at Hare who had never agreed on anything before, and the miller’s boy at Tin Jack, who was late leaving and then decided not to bother.
The soldiers ran. The ringers didn’t. The Warden noticed that, and kept it.
The next morning, Vreni stood looking at his empty hands.
“You need something to hit them with.”
“I was not given anything.”
“Then I’ll give you something.”

She fetched Ottmar the smith, who had stayed with his sick wife. They lowered the Gate Bell from the tower, and Ottmar broke it and melted it down into a hammer head the size of a cart. For the haft he used the oak beam it had hung from for three hundred years.
Vreni watched the bronze run out of the furnace like honey. Her family had rung that bell for seven generations.
“It’s still mine,” she told the Warden, when they set the hammer in his hands. “You give it back after.”
“I will.”
On the fourth morning she climbed a tower with no bell in it and shouted first light into the empty air. Down the valley, the six bells answered anyway. Then the Ashen Host came up the pass.

sections.heading: III. The Ninth Night
paragraphs: At the gate the pass was twelve men wide, and the Host came twelve at a time, day and night, for nine days.

The Warden didn’t sleep, because stone doesn’t. He didn’t hurry, because he didn’t need to. Every swing of the hammer rang the Gate Bell’s note, and the Host learned to hate that sound. By the fourth day the snow was red for a mile.
Every morning Vreni shouted the hour from the tower over forty thousand heads, and the six bells answered, Tin Jack last.

On the ninth night the Host stopped coming and started building. They stacked pines against the Warden’s legs and burned them all night, an old miners’ trick for breaking rock. Just before dawn they emptied every cauldron in the camp over him, full of snowmelt.
His left knee split with a crack like a bell breaking.
Then they brought up a ram, a whole pine shod in iron with sixty men on it, and drove it into the crack.

Stone doesn’t feel pain. What the Warden felt was worse: the slow, certain lean of something that has stood a very long time and is about to stop. He was tipping backward into the arch. And a wall lying down is only a ramp.
Something small hit the back of his knee. Vreni had come down from the tower in her grandfather’s coat. She put her back against the crack, dug her heels into the snow, and pushed.
“Move,” he said. It was the first word he had spoken in nine days.
“No.”
“Vreni. I am falling. Move.”
She set her jaw the way she did on the coldest mornings. “Move me.”
He couldn’t. To move her he would have to let go of the gate. To fall, he would have to fall on her. There was nowhere left for him to go but up.

He brought the hammer down on the road in front of him and hauled himself upright by it, the way an old man gets up with a stick. The Gate Bell struck the mountain, and the mountain split. A crack ran out from the hammer’s head across the pass, a mile long and as deep as a well, and the fires and the ram and the sixty men went into it.
Then the Warden roared, for the first time in three hundred years. It came out of him as the Gate Bell’s note, and down the valley six bells rang by themselves with nobody touching a rope.

sections.heading: IV. Seven Bells
paragraphs: On the tenth morning she climbed the hundred and nine steps with her hands shaking and called the hour.
“First light, and the pass holds!”
The Widow answered. Then Kettle, then Hare, then Long Tom, then Little Agnes. Then, last as always, Tin Jack.
Across the fissure, the Ashen Host listened to the bells ring down the valley for the tenth morning in a row. Then they turned around and went home.

The valley came home to find the Warden cracked in eleven places. Nobody knew how to mend a mountain. Ottmar said gold might do it: it never rusts, and it gives a little without breaking. So the valley brought him their gold: wedding rings, a saint’s medal, the gilt off the chapel cross, a widow’s savings in a sock. Ottmar hammered it into bands and riveted them around every crack. The thickest is on his left knee.
When it was done, the Warden held the hammer out to Vreni.
“I said I would give it back.”
The hammer was chipped and stained to the haft, and it was not a bell anymore.
“Does it still ring?”
He touched it to the stone. It rang: the Gate Bell’s note, a little lower, the way a voice goes lower when someone is tired.
“Keep it,” she said. “Ring it for me.”
So for a hundred years the valley rang its six remaining bells at first light, and when Tin Jack had finished, late as ever, the Warden struck the road once with his hammer, and the seventh answered.

Vreni rang the hour for seventy-one years. She married one of the brothers from Hare, outlived him, and taught her granddaughter the hundred and nine steps. Every morning after the call, she put her shoulder to the Warden’s gold knee and pushed. He never moved.

The last morning she climbed the tower, she was eighty-one, and it took her most of an hour. Afterwards she came down very slowly and laid her hand on his gold knee. She didn’t push. She didn’t have the strength left.
The Warden took one step back.

It was the only step backward he had taken in nearly four hundred years. Vreni laughed until she had to sit down in the snow. Then he stepped forward again into the arch where he belonged, and she went home. She died that winter. He rang for her every morning after.

sections.heading: V. The Unmoving Wall
paragraphs: The valley is empty now. A trade road came through the pass, the young went down it to the market towns, and one by one the towers fell quiet. Tin Jack was the last bell to go, sold to a lowland church. It was late leaving, as usual.
For years after, he rang the morning alone. Caravans passed under his arm. Nobody came to try him.

The priests had told him to hold the pass. Vreni had shown him what it was for. When the last of them had gone down the road, there was nothing left up there to hold, so he went after them. Every village he passed came out to watch, because nobody had ever seen a mountain walk.

In the duelling rings the heralds call him Khalvar of the Seven Bells, and the crowds call him the Unmoving Wall. He is slow, and doesn’t need to be anything else. A blade on stone is just weather. He lets them come, and when they are close the hammer comes down, the Gate Bell rings, and the floor splits under them in a long line, the way the pass did on the ninth night. When he roars, the stands hear a bell.
He came because a wall with nothing against it is just a rock on a hill, and he wants to know if anything can do what forty thousand men could not.

And he likes the fighters. That was the other half of what he learned in the pass: people break so easily, and they come anyway. Stone is never brave. It doesn’t have to be. The ones who walk up to him are.
Before every bout he plants his feet, looks down at whoever has come to try, and says the one thing anyone ever said to him that he had no answer for.
“Move me.”

Nobody has. At first light, wherever he is, he strikes the ground once and lets the Gate Bell ring, and if you stand close you can hear the millstone voice under it, calling the hour to an empty valley. First light, and the pass holds.
Only one person ever moved him. She was eighty-one, and she didn’t even have to push.
